source.authors: Finnerty PB, Possell M, Banks PB, Orlando CG, Price CJ, Shrader AM, McArthur C
source.title: Olfactory misinformation provides refuge to palatable plants from mammalian browsing

value: free-ranging swamp wallabies browsed Eucalyptus punctata seedlings no more often when the seedling was ringed by dispensers releasing a seven-compound odour mimic of the unpalatable shrub Boronia pinnata than when ringed by real B. pinnata plants (P = 0.72), so the odour mixture alone gave the same browsing refuge
units: categorical (time to first browse of a seedling, Cox proportional-hazards model; treatment pairwise comparison, P value)
method: field experiment: one nursery-grown E. punctata seedling (325 +/- 18 mm) at the centre of each of 90 plots (six treatments, 15 plots each, plots at least 50 m apart, completely randomised); five neighbours on a 1 m radius circle were real B. pinnata shrubs, dispensers releasing the informative seven-VOC mixture (in B. pinnata proportions), dispensers with an uninformative odour, dispensers with the flipped-proportion mixture, empty dispensers (procedural control) or none; motion-triggered infrared cameras recorded browsing for a 40-day main trial in February-March 2023 after a 14-day pre-trial
conditions: wild-sourced: free-ranging swamp wallabies (Wallabia bicolor) browsing in eucalypt woodland in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, Sydney (odour sampling site; the paper does not say where the main trial plots lay), individuals not identified and wallaby density not reported; only a relative background-activity score per site from the pre-trial, which did not differ among treatments (LR chi-square 1.90, P = 0.86); the seedlings and the real neighbour shrubs were nursery-sourced plants, not wild; dispensers did not significantly change the emitted VOCs (R = 0.092, P = 0.13); 82 seedlings were browsed overall and 75 of those had all foliage eaten, with no per-treatment count printed in the text; hazard ratios are pairwise, the exact values being in Extended Data Table 2 which the reader did not return; plots, not wallabies, are the unit; weather in the 40 days: 12 rain days, 13.3 to 37.0 C
where: Results, browsing refuge from virtual neighbours (main text)
quote: Informative virtual neighbours provided real browsing refuge from swamp wallabies, equivalent to protection provided by real B. pinnata plants (P = 0.72).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, wild herbivore choice (time to first browse) at odour-releasing dispensers against no-odour and procedural controls in the field; the value says the informative VOC mixture matched real neighbours for refuge and does not establish which compounds or which sense organ carry the effect. Same-paper contrary and secondary results: seedlings with no neighbours were 20 times more likely to be browsed than seedlings ringed by informative virtual neighbours and 17 times more likely than those ringed by real B. pinnata (both P < 0.0001, Cox hazard ratios); seedlings ringed by flipped-proportion odour, uninformative odour or empty dispensers were equally likely to be browsed as seedlings alone, so no refuge from those three treatments (values in Extended Data Table 2, not returned). source.authors: Grocock NL, Batallas RE, McNamara EA, Sturm AB, Manson JS, Evenden ML
source.title: Bumble Bees (Hymenoptera: Apidae) Respond to Moth (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae) Pheromone Components Leading to Bee Bycatch in Monitoring Traps Targeting Moth Pests

value: wild free-flying B. rufocinctus (worker and queen females) were captured in significantly greater numbers per trap in Unitraps baited with noctuid moth pheromone lures than in unbaited control traps (2014 field season; lure-type effect Wald chi-square = 60.949, df = 4, p < 0.0001)
units: categorical (bees captured per trap; lure-type effect by Wald chi-square, pairwise comparison with unbaited control by Tukey letters in Figure 1)
method: field trapping: non-saturating green Unitraps 1.5 m above ground, 25 m apart on a roadside field-edge transect at each of seven sites in five central Alberta counties (sites at least 20 km apart, each a canola and a wheat field at least 500 m apart); five lure treatments deployed concurrently 23 June to 2 September 2014: a food bait of acetic acid and 3-methyl-1-butanol (1:1, 10 mL), pheromone lures for redbacked cutworm, bertha armyworm and true armyworm, and an unbaited control trap in each field; pheromone lures replaced every 4 weeks and food bait every 2 weeks, trap contents collected weekly
conditions: wild-sourced: free-flying wild bumble bees (B. rufocinctus) captured at central Alberta canola and wheat field edges, females only (males excluded from identification and analysis); the paper does not state the number of traps per lure treatment or the replicate count and says only that transects were placed on a random edge of each field, so how trap positions were allocated is unclear; the quoted sentence pools the noctuid pheromone lures (three species' pheromone lures in 2014) and the pairwise contrasts with the control are shown only as Tukey letters in Figure 1; insecticide strips were used in the traps and replaced every 4 weeks; individual bees are not identified so a trap, not a bee, is the unit; capture in a trap measures attraction, not the sense organ used
quote: There were significantly more B. rufocinctus per trap captured in the noctuid moth pheromone-baited Unitraps than in unbaited control traps (Figure 1).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, attraction of wild bees to synthetic moth sex-pheromone lures (trap catch against an unbaited control) in the field; the value says wild B. rufocinctus come to pheromone-baited traps and does not say the bees use the pheromone as a communication signal. Same-paper contrary and secondary results: in 2014 B. rufocinctus capture did not differ between unbaited control traps and traps baited with the food bait lure (acetic acid and 3-methyl-1-butanol); in 2015 (nine treatments, 29 June-4 August) among the pheromone lures only the pale western cutworm pheromone captured significantly more B. rufocinctus than the control, adding phenylacetaldehyde to the food bait raised capture and the floral food bait was significantly above the control, and capture was higher at canola than wheat (p = 0.006); in 2016 (six treatments, 7 June-28 July) phenylacetaldehyde alone caught the most, the redbacked cutworm and bertha armyworm pheromones caught significantly more than the control, the original food bait and the dead-moth treatment did not differ from the control, and the canola-wheat difference was not significant (p = 0.095); the electroantennogram tests in the paper used wild B. rufocinctus workers (and commercial-colony B. impatiens) and were not filed; B. rufocinctus did not respond to Z11-16Ac at any tested concentration.
